To: Executive Leadership Team
From: Sustainability & Logistics Director
Date: Today
Subject: Balanced shipping plan to control cost and reduce carbon footprint under real-world operating rules

Context
We move finished goods from a network of warehouses to a network of retail stores. Each shipping route has two per‑unit performance metrics: monetary cost and carbon emissions. In practice, the least‑cost lanes tend to carry a higher emissions intensity, and cleaner options often cost more. Customers, regulators, and investors expect measurable progress on sustainability, while the business must protect margin and on‑shelf availability. We will therefore evaluate shipping decisions against a blended measure of cost and emissions, and produce a practical plan that keeps service whole.

Operational rules we must respect
- Route activation costs: Opening a route triggers a one‑time setup charge that covers contracts, compliance work, and dock preparation. A route is either active or not; once active, that fee applies regardless of volume moved on that lane.
- Minimum order quantities: Activated routes must carry at least a specified minimum volume to justify truck utilization and terminal handling; partial loads below that threshold are not permitted.
- Supplier limits per store: Each store’s receiving capacity and vendor governance cap the number of warehouses that may deliver to it. This prevents over‑fragmentation at the dock and simplifies store‑side scheduling and invoicing.

Supply and demand guardrails
- Warehouses can only ship up to their available inventory; no location will be planned beyond its supply.
- Each store has a required intake to maintain availability; plans must cover at least that demand.
- The mix of lanes must observe both the minimum‑per‑lane requirement and the cap on how many warehouses supply any given store.

Management priority and how we will score options
Leadership has defined the relative importance of cost and emissions. We will apply those importance weights to the variable portion of shipping cost and to total emissions to produce a single blended score for each plan. Setup fees for activated lanes will be added in full as spend, not scaled by these weights. This scoring lets us compare realistic plans on a common basis and make clear, defensible trade‑offs.

Business goal and decision output
Our goal is to identify which routes to activate and how many units to ship on each active route so that:
- Warehouse inventory is not exceeded and store demand is met.
- Activated routes satisfy their minimum volume.
- Each store is served by no more than the allowed number of warehouses.
- The resulting plan achieves the lowest blended total of weighted variable cost and weighted emissions, plus all setup fees for the routes we activate.

What you can expect
- A recommended shipping plan: activated lanes and shipment quantities by lane.
- A summary of projected spend, projected emissions, and operational feasibility checks (supply utilization, store coverage, lane MOQs, supplier caps).
- Sensitivity views showing how the recommendation changes if leadership adjusts the importance weights, route setups, or minimums.
- Clear call‑outs where a small increase in spend materially improves carbon performance, or where we can lower emissions with negligible impact on cost.
